body.x: In the pre-CES 2024 online meetup hosted by AVING News on the 21st, Nuvilab (CEO Dae Hoon Kim) presented its food tech solution 'AI Food Scanner' to Hubert Nguyen from Ubergizmo. In the 30-minute meetup, Nuvilab introduced its newest product, which the company plans to showcase to visitors at CES 2024, and then answered questions from Ubergizmo's Hubert.

Nuvilab said it integrates vision-based AI food recognition technology and extensive data analysis to calculate the amount of food waste generated. The main problem Nuvilab tackles in the sustainability domain is the need for more data optimization in the food industry centered around food prices, nutrition insecurity, and carbon emissions.

Nuvilab's global business development manager, Ayden, who presented on behalf of his company, said, "We are glad to be able to introduce our newly updated product and software, which we dubbed the 'dataware for food services.' After a couple of updates from 2018, when we began, and up until now, we have successfully accumulated a ton of data. I will not lay out the number, but we have successfully proved our model accuracy to be 95% in both classification and volume estimation."

In Korea, Nuvilab's initial strategy was to target key sectors, such as the Ministry of National Defense, schools, and preschools, in collaboration with the government. The company broadened its reach by partnering with various hospitality groups and food service companies, including Aramark Korea, to offer solutions to different food service operators. In 6th year as a startup aiming for global expansion, Nuvilab said its vision-based AI food recognition and extensive data analysis pinpoint the amount of waste generated, addressing the crucial problem of data optimization in the food industry.

Nuvilab said its AI Food Scanner showcasing at CES 2024 employs an advanced vision AI technology that performs food analysis in just 0.97 seconds, identifying the type and quantity of food on trays and bins to prevent overproduction and reduce carbon emissions.

"What's changed is that it is much more modular and flexible. So, traditionally, we had one model with RGB and depth information. And then now we have a central computer model, the RGB sensor that will be mounted on the top, and then the depth sensor mounted on the bottom. So, per the client's need, it will be the same hardware design. That can be modulated and must be pretty flexible per client," Nuvilab's Ayden said.

"So our technology, again," Nuvilab's Ayden continued, "implements AI and 3D depth sensors to enable accurate processing in real time to infer what type and amount of food item is being presented. This is one of the examples where we implement this technology in the halls. So, the individuals would scan their plates. Then, the AI will infer which items are present, and then the depth analysis will infer how many of what items are being presented.

"It is 3D vision computer provision. It seamlessly integrates into the preexisting kitchen environment or the hall environment. So, in the traditional methods, it would have to weigh the individual trays or the food disposal bins. By implementing vision sensors, we don't need those big hardware to scale or measure those food items. Then, we also allow the food consumption and waste output levels of each food item presented, which can only be succeeded by those vision sensors.

"So first implementation is what we've been doing for the past five years. It's a food tray scanner so that an individual can scan their tray, and then they would know how much they have left and how much carbon output or nutrition intake they have consumed. And then the second thing is relatively new. It has been showcased in a couple of events previously, but it is more focused on the kitchen operation, so instead of scanning the trays, it would be watching the trash bins. The output is the same so that it would give out the information on the depth and the type of the food items. But then, it is more focused on kitchen operation and management so they can better control their stocks. They can predict their covers and the number of diners better. The last one is the automated conveyor and scanner. It is the smallest scanner we have; it will be mounted on the conveyor belt where the environment allows, and then it will automatically scan all the food items being left.

"So the depth of the information we give out has been optimized for each client. Before, it was how much food, nutrition, and waste, but now, we can modulate that for particular needs, depending on the patient's condition and the facility in terms of hospital or long-term care. They can have their models that they can implement. Then, we will have dashboards to optimize and filter through that information.

"As said for different purposes, we have dubbed our solutions for more clarity. So, the diet manager will be our previous nutrition intake manager. So, anything related to nutritional intake and diet control ranges from educational facilities to military long-term care and hospitals. All things related to nutrition and intake will be integrated into the diet manager program. The second thing is that a footprint manager is pretty. Self-explanatory is what we've been doing. And then it's the most substantial basis that we have. It will calculate how much carbon emission is being put out for that specific client or facility. And we're cooperating with Fao and other international organizations to clarify better how to calculate that carbon emission.

"And then, the last thing is the inventory manager. This is geared towards the kitchen so the kitchen managers would have better clarity. In terms of understanding what they need to purchase more, what they need to buy less, and what they can expect regarding the number of customers and diners, our Dataware is designed to enhance the preexisting operators—clarity and data management control a couple of use cases."

Looking ahead to CES 2024, Nuvilab plans to operate a 1,500-square-foot booth, a significant undertaking for a startup. The company hopes the opportunity will allow it to connect more relevantly with our existing and potential clients in diverse sectors as we continue to showcase the impactful role of AI in everyday health, dietary management, and food waste management.

Nuvilab, having secured Series A funding last October, made an impactful debut at CES 2023, attracting attention from prominent companies like Aramark and Sodexo. At CES 2024, it will showcase its innovative solutions, including the AI Food Scanner 3.0 and various management tools (Kitchen Manager, Hall Manager, and Care Manager). These solutions aim to assist in managing Type 2 Diabetes diets and promote sustainability efforts towards net zero. With a strategic focus on expanding into the American and European markets, Nuvilab said it aspires to make significant advancements in these regions.
